PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
PREPARED IN ANTICIPATION OF LITIGATION

MEMORANDUM

TO: Engagement Team — Antitrust & Competition
FROM: Antitrust & Competition Group
DATE: August 10, 2026
RE: Antitrust Risk Assessment and HSR Filing Strategy — Industrial Gas Distribution Acquisition (PE Acquisition with Horizontal Overlap)

I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This memorandum provides (i) an assessment of antitrust risk associated with the proposed acquisition of an industrial gas distribution business by a private equity sponsor whose portfolio includes an existing industrial gas distribution platform, (ii) a recommended Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act of 1976 ("HSR Act") filing strategy, and (iii) a line-by-line reconciliation of the counterparty's latest markup against the base agreement materials, flagging every deviation and providing negotiating recommendations consistent with client directives.

The transaction presents a substantive horizontal overlap in the industrial gas distribution market. Independent of the HSR notification threshold analysis, the parties share overlapping product and geographic markets, warranting a rigorous antitrust risk assessment. The HSR filing is required (size-of-transaction threshold met), and the recommended fee tier depends on the total "acquisition value" defined under HSR regulations, which includes cash consideration, funded debt assumed or refinanced, and the maximum contingent earnout payable.

The counterparty markup introduces four material deviations from the base agreement: (1) a silent reduction of the indemnification cap; (2) conversion of the basket from a deductible to a tipping basket; (3) expansion of the Material Adverse Effect ("MAE") definition to include carve-outs for regulatory action; and (4) a shortened survival period for core representations. Per the controlling partner directive, the basket conversion is acceptable as a concession; the survival-period reduction is a walk-away issue and must be rejected. The indemnification cap reduction and MAE carve-out expansion require further analysis and negotiation.

II. TRANSACTION OVERVIEW

A. Parties and Structure

The transaction involves a private equity sponsor (the "Buyer") acquiring a target company engaged in industrial gas distribution (the "Target"). The Buyer's portfolio includes an existing industrial gas distribution platform (the "Platform"), creating a direct horizontal overlap between the Buyer's existing operations and the Target's business.

This is a stock purchase transaction in which the Buyer will acquire all issued and outstanding equity interests of the Target. The operative agreement contains representations and warranties, covenants, conditions precedent to closing, indemnification provisions, and termination rights.

B. Transaction Consideration

The aggregate consideration is comprised of cash consideration payable at closing, plus any funded debt assumed or refinanced in connection with the closing, and the maximum contingent earnout amount, if any. Under HSR regulations, the "acquisition value" for purposes of determining the applicable filing fee is the sum of these components (cash consideration + funded debt assumed/refinanced + maximum contingent earnout). Cash on the Target's balance sheet at closing is not deducted from the acquisition value; a deal's headline "purchase price" customarily quotes cash consideration only and does not represent the reportable acquisition value for HSR purposes.

The precise acquisition value is established by the fully executed agreement and any addenda. Should the acquisition value fall at or above the HSR notification threshold (currently $119.5 million for 2026), the parties must file HSR notifications.

III. ANTITRUST RISK ASSESSMENT

A. Horizontal Overlap Analysis

The Buyer's existing industrial gas distribution platform and the Target operate in the same product and geographic markets. The horizontal overlap raises substantive antitrust concerns that the reviewing agencies (the Federal Trade Commission ("FTC") and the Antitrust Division of the Department of Justice ("DOJ")) will assess under Section 7 of the Clayton Act (15 U.S.C. § 18) and Section 1 of the Sherman Act at the conclusion of the HSR waiting period.

1. Product Market

Industrial gas distribution includes the production, liquefaction, storage, and last-mile delivery of atmospheric gases (nitrogen, oxygen, argon) and specialty/process gases (hydrogen, helium, carbon dioxide, acetylene) to end users in manufacturing, healthcare, food and beverage, semiconductor, metals fabrication, and chemical processing industries. The relevant product market definition will likely be characterized by:
- Bulk/liquid gas supply versus packaged/cylinder gas distribution;
- Merchant supply versus on-site/captive supply; and
- Geographic scope of distribution networks (regional pipeline, local cylinder distribution, national logistics).

2. Geographic Market

Industrial gas distribution is often viewed through a regional lens, particularly for bulk liquid delivery where transport economics are constrained by distance from production plants and distribution terminals. Packaged gas distribution may have broader geographic reach but faces local competitive dynamics. The FTC and DOJ will analyze the relevant geographic market based on supply and demand substitution, the location of production facilities, and customer switching patterns.

3. Concentration Assessment

The Buyer and Target compete directly in the relevant industrial gas distribution markets. Post-transaction market concentration will be evaluated using the HHI (Herfindahl-Hirschman Index) framework under the 2023 Merger Guidelines (Justice Department & FTC, December 18, 2023). If the post-merger HHI exceeds 1,800 and the transaction increases the HHI by more than 100 points, the transaction will be presumed to raise competitive concerns absent rebuttal evidence.

B. Regulatory Exposure

The counterparty markup adds carve-outs to the MAE definition for "regulatory action." Critically, Schedule 3.7 to the base agreement discloses two pending regulatory inquiries involving the Target. These inquiries could relate to antitrust review of the transaction, environmental permitting requirements for gas distribution facilities, or other regulatory compliance matters. The interaction between the MAE carve-outs and the known regulatory inquiries creates a risk allocation issue: the counterparty seeks to exclude losses or adverse effects arising from regulatory action from MAE triggers, while the Buyer's counsel will need to assess whether such carve-outs inappropriately transfer regulatory risk to the Buyer.

C. Risk Rating

Overall antitrust risk is assessed as MODERATE-to-ELEVATED. Key risk factors include:
- Direct horizontal overlap in industrial gas distribution
- Potential for post-merger market shares that exceed agency guidelines
- Geographic overlap in key distribution markets
- Two pending regulatory inquiries (per Schedule 3.7) that invite agency scrutiny
- The Buyer's status as a private equity sponsor with a portfolio platform in the same market

Mitigating factors include:
- Potential for entry by other industrial gas distributors
- The competitive presence of large national players (e.g., Linde, Air Products, Air Liquide) that may constrain pricing
- The possibility that the relevant geographic markets are sufficiently broad to reduce concentration

D. Recommended Risk Mitigation Measures

1. Conduct a thorough market-share and concentration analysis for the overlapping product and geographic markets.
2. Prepare a merger-specific efficiencies submission (cost savings in distribution logistics, reduced delivery costs, expanded service coverage).
3. Consider proactively offering a divestiture or behavioral remedies should the agencies screen the transaction.
4. Document the competitive rationale for the acquisition for production in response to any requested CIDs (Civil Investigative Demands).

IV. HSR FILING STRATEGY

A. Filing Obligation

The HSR Act requires premerger notification filings with the FTC and DOJ for transactions that exceed the current size-of-transaction threshold (in 2026, $119.5 million) unless an exemption applies. Based on the acquisition value considerations described above, the transaction is reportable.

B. Acquisition Value Calculation and Fee Determination

Under HSR regulations, the acquisition value is the total consideration the buyer gives up:
- Cash consideration;
- Funded debt assumed or refinanced at closing; and
- The maximum contingent earnout payable.

Cash on the target's balance sheet at closing is NOT deducted from the acquisition value. The headline "purchase price" customarily quoted in press releases (which reflects only cash consideration) is not the reportable acquisition value.

The applicable fee is determined by the tier into which the acquisition value falls:

  $119,500,000 to < $173,300,000 ...... $30,000
  $173,300,000 to < $536,500,000 ...... $105,000
  $536,500,000 to < $1,073,000,000 .... $260,000
  $1,073,000,000 to < $2,146,000,000 .. $415,000
  $2,146,000,000 and above ............ $2,335,000

C. Timing and Procedural Strategy

1. Early HSR Filing Window. If possible, file within 30 days of signing to start the 30-day initial waiting period early. The parties may request early termination, which is often granted for transactions presenting no substantive competitive concerns.

2. Second Request Preparedness. Given the horizontal overlap, the agencies may issue a Second Request that extends the waiting period. The parties should anticipate this possibility and prepare:
   - Custodians and document collection plan;
   - Customer, supplier, and competitor interview readiness;
   - Answering capacity for CID data requests, including market share data, sales by product and geography, strategic planning documents, and competitive analyses.

3. Substantive Interaction Strategy. Strategically engaging with the FTC/DOJ early (pre-filing) is recommended to surface and address competition concerns before the formal waiting period begins. Where horizontal overlap exists, pre-filing discussion often shortens the substantive review timeline.

4. Divestiture Contingency. If the agencies raise presumptive concentration concerns, the parties should be prepared to discuss a carve-out divestiture package for overlapping assets or customer contracts, or to agree to behavioral commitments (e.g., firewall provisions, supply obligations).

D. Recommended Filing Fee Budget

Based on the anticipated acquisition value (to be confirmed from the executed deal documents), the filing fee should be reserved in the matter budget at the tier corresponding to the total reportable acquisition value. The fee should be recorded as the matter's filing fee budget line item.

V. COUNTERPARTY MARKUP RECONCILIATION

The counterparty has circulated a markup of the base agreement. This section reconciles each deviation against the base materials and provides a recommended position consistent with the client's directives.

A. Deviation 1: Indemnification Cap (Section 8.2)

Base Material Position: The base agreement contains an indemnification cap applicable to breaches of representations and warranties (excluding fundamental representations, which are capped at the full purchase price, and fraud).

Counterparty Markup Position: The counterparty's markup silently reduces the indemnification cap from the firm-standard level.

Analysis: A reduced indemnification cap materially shifts post-closing risk to the Buyer by limiting the Seller's exposure for breaches of representations and warranties. The reduction is not accompanied by any commensurate reduction in the purchase price or other adjustment. This is a one-sided risk-shifting proposal.

Additional Consideration — Schedule 5.2: The schedules to the base agreement disclose certain retained liabilities. If the cap is reduced, the Buyer's ability to recover for losses arising from retained liabilities disclosed on Schedule 5.2 is further impaired. The schedule's retained liabilities intersect directly with the indemnification cap reduction, as the losses attributable to those retained liabilities would need to be recovered from the cap, potentially exhausting it entirely.

Recommendation: REJECT the cap reduction. The Buyer should hold firm on the base agreement's cap level and should not accept a reduced cap without a corresponding purchase price adjustment, increased escrow, or additional indemnity. The retained liabilities in Schedule 5.2 underscore the need to maintain the cap at the base level to preserve meaningful recovery rights.

B. Deviation 2: Basket Conversion — Deductible to Tipping Basket (Section 8.3)

Base Material Position: The base agreement provides for a true deductible: the Seller has no liability until aggregate losses exceed a stated threshold, and then the Seller is liable only for losses in excess of the deductible.

Counterparty Markup Position: The counterparty's markup converts the basket from a deductible to a "tipping basket" (or "first-dollar" basket): once aggregate losses exceed the stated threshold, the Seller becomes liable for ALL losses from the first dollar, not just those in excess of the basket amount.

Analysis: A tipping basket is favorable to the Buyer because it provides recovery for losses below the threshold once the aggregate threshold is crossed. However, this change likely arose from the counterparty's attempt to balance other shifts in the agreement; alternatively, it may be an error.

Client Directive: Per the controlling partner instruction, the client WILL CONCEDE the basket conversion from a deductible to a tipping basket. This is an accepted position and should not be contested.

Recommendation: ACCEPT the basket conversion per the partner directive. The client has determined this is a concession the deal team is willing to make. No further pushback should be made on this point.

C. Deviation 3: MAE Definition — Regulatory Action Carve-Outs (Section 1.1 / Definition)

Base Material Position: The base agreement's MAE definition follows the customary two-part structure, with carve-outs for general economic/financial market conditions, conditions affecting the industry, changes in law or GAAP, epidemics/pandemics, acts of war/terrorism/natural disasters, the announcement or pendency of the transactions, and failure to meet projections. The disproportionate-impact modifier applies to certain carve-outs.

Counterparty Markup Position: The counterparty's markup ADDS new carve-outs to the MAE definition for regulatory action. Specifically, the markup seeks to exclude from MAE triggers any adverse effects arising from "regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter."

Analysis: This deviation is particularly concerning because Schedule 3.7 to the base agreement discloses two pending regulatory inquiries involving the Target. The counterparty appears to be attempting to pre-emptively carve out the consequences of those known regulatory proceedings from the MAE definition. If accepted, this would mean that:
(1) adverse outcomes from those pending regulatory inquiries would not constitute MAEs that would allow the Buyer to walk from the transaction; and
(2) the Buyer would be forced to close the transaction even if a material regulatory adverse development occurred post-signing.

The timing is critical: the counterparty is seeking to write a carve-out that protects against risks it already knows exist (per Schedule 3.7 disclosures). This is a significant deviation that fundamentally reallocates regulatory risk.

Recommendation: REJECT the regulatory-action MAE carve-out, or at minimum, narrow it significantly. Any carve-out for regulatory action should be limited to actions first arising after the signing date and should expressly exclude the two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed in Schedule 3.7. If the counterparty insists on a regulatory carve-out, the Buyer should condition its acceptance on a requirement that the Seller disclose all known regulatory investigations and indemnify the Buyer for losses arising from the known Schedule 3.7 inquiries.

D. Deviation 4: Survival Period — Reduction for Core Representations (Section 8.1)

Base Material Position: Exhibit B to the base agreement sets the survival matrix, which provides that certain representations survive for specified periods. The base agreement follows the firm-standard survival framework for representations and warranties.

Counterparty Markup Position: The counterparty's markup introduces a new limitation period that shortens the survival period for the core representations (excluding fundamental representations and, in the case of the base deal, tax representations that survive until 60 days after expiration of the statute of limitations).

Analysis: Shortening the survival period for core representations materially reduces the Buyer's ability to bring post-closing indemnification claims. This interacts with the indemnification cap reduction (Deviation 1) to create a "double squeeze": lower cap plus shorter window to identify and assert claims. The deviation directly contradicts Exhibit B, which is a scheduled annex that controls over the general agreement text.

Client Directive: Per the controlling partner instruction, the client treats ANY survival-period reduction as a WALK-AWAY ISSUE. This is the client's hard-line position. Deal failure is preferred over accepting a shortened survival period.

Recommendation: REJECT the survival-period reduction absolutely. This is a walk-away issue per the client's directive. The deal team should communicate that the survival periods in Exhibit B are non-negotiable and, if the counterparty persists, the transaction may not proceed.

VI. KEY RISK OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDED NEXT STEPS

A. Counterparty Markup Risk Accumulation

The counterparty's markup seeks to make three simultaneous risk-shifting changes to the Buyer's detriment:
1. Reduced indemnification cap;
2. Expanded MAE carve-outs for regulatory action (including known regulatory inquiries); and
3. Shortened survival period for core representations.

The basket conversion (from deductible to tipping) is the only change favorable to the Buyer, and the client has directed that this be conceded.

B. Walk-Away Issue Identification

The survival-period reduction is the controlling walk-away issue per partner instruction. If the counterparty does not retreat on this point, the transaction should not proceed. The deal team should escalate this issue immediately if there is any indication the counterparty will hold firm.

C. Recommended Elevation Path

1. Communicate the client's positions on the four deviations to the counterparty in a consolidated redline response.
2. Negotiate the MAE carve-out and indemnification cap changes before agreeing to a definitive agreement.
3. If the counterparty pushes back on survival periods, escalate to client decision-makers and consider termination.

VII. CONCLUSION

The proposed industrial gas distribution acquisition presents a reportable HSR transaction with a substantive horizontal overlap requiring careful antitrust scrutiny. While the deal is likely to be approved by the agencies (subject to potential second request review or remedies discussion), the counterparty's markup introduces several material deviations that must be addressed before the parties can proceed.

The team should: (a) confirm the acquisition value and file the HSR notification with the appropriate fee; (b) prepare a Second Request readiness plan; (c) reject the indemnification cap reduction and MAE carve-out expansion; (d) accept the basket conversion per partner directive; and (e) treat any survival-period shortening as a walk-away issue.

Respectfully submitted,

[Antitrust & Competition Group]
[Simulated Law Firm]
